summary: Defines text/enriched, a MIME content type for simple formatted text so basic enriched text works across many kinds of hardware and software. It refines text/richtext from RFC 1341. It was replaced by RFC 1896.

eli5.summary: Plain text is like writing with one pen. This memo lets you use bold and slanted words that show up on any computer.

questions: how do you add bold or italic to email
how does text/enriched handle different character sets
what happened to text/enriched after it was replaced
subtitle: Simple formatting markup for email that works on any system.

tldr.problem: Email systems could send plain text or fancy formatted text, but there was no standard way to send simple formatting like bold or italics that would work everywhere.
tldr.mechanism: text/enriched defines a MIME content type with a simple syntax for formatting: commands in angle brackets mark where bold, italic, and other formatting begin and end. The syntax is simple enough that even text-only email systems can strip out the markup and show readable plain text.
tldr.outcome: The format allowed richer email while remaining widely compatible, though it was replaced by RFC 1896 as email capabilities evolved. It served as a bridge between plain text email and more advanced formatting systems.

facts.label: Formatting commands
facts.value: Multiple categories: font, fill, indent, misc

facts.label: Nesting requirement
facts.value: All commands must be properly balanced

today: RFC 1563 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 1896. It provided a simple, portable way to add basic formatting to email, though modern email systems use richer formats like HTML. The design principles of graceful degradation and simplicity remain relevant to protocol design.

sections.title: Simple Formatting for Email
sections.content:
RFC 1563 defines text/enriched, a MIME content type for simple formatted text designed to work across many different hardware and software platforms. It refines the earlier text/richtext type from RFC 1341, simplifying and clarifying the specification. The design goals were ambitious: the syntax must be simple to parse (even teletype systems could strip it), extensible for future commands, readable even to non-MIME mail readers, and limited in capability to what most word processors could represent.

The name change from "richtext" to "enriched" reflects both a simplification and a distinction from Microsoft's Rich Text Format (RTF), which caused confusion. Text/enriched fills a middle ground: more capable than plain text, yet far simpler and more portable than binary formats like ODA or proprietary word processor formats.
sections.eli5: A new mail type lets you add bold and slanted words to email in a way that works on any computer, even very old ones that do not support fancy formatting.

sections.title: The Format and Syntax
sections.content:
Text/enriched uses a minimal syntax centered on angle brackets. All characters represent themselves except for the less-than sign ('<'), which marks the start of a formatting command. Commands are enclosed in angle brackets: <commandname> begins an effect and </commandname> ends it. Commands are case-insensitive, so <bold> and <BOLD> are equivalent. To represent a literal less-than sign, you use two: <<.

All formatting commands must be properly balanced and nested: if you start <bold>, you must close it with </bold> before ending any outer formatting like <italic>. Commands may be no more than 60 characters long and use only alphanumeric characters and hyphens. Unrecognized commands are simply ignored, allowing mail systems to gracefully handle future extensions they do not understand.
sections.eli5: Formatting uses angle brackets like angle brackets <bold>text</bold>. You close them in the opposite order you opened them, like closing parentheses.

sections.title: Formatting Commands and Capabilities
sections.content:
The RFC defines several categories of formatting commands. Font-alteration commands change text appearance: <bold>, <italic>, <fixed> (monospace), <smaller>, <bigger>, and <underline>. Fill and justification commands control text wrapping and alignment: <center>, <flushleft>, <flushright>, <flushboth> (full justify), and <nofill> (preserve line breaks). Indentation commands adjust margins: <indent> and <indentright>. Miscellaneous commands include <excerpt> (for quoted text) and <param> (for hidden parameters used by extensions).

Line breaks are handled specially: a single line break becomes a space, but multiple consecutive line breaks are preserved as line breaks minus one. This allows mail to be wrapped at 80 characters during transport without breaking the intended layout. The initial state assumes filled text in a variable-width font, left and right margins at maximum, and normal font size.
sections.eli5: You can make text bold, italic, or in a fixed font; center it or line it up left or right; and indent it. Line breaks work like in normal text.

sections.title: Interoperability and Extensions
sections.content:
One of the key design goals was to ensure that text/enriched mail would remain readable even on systems that do not support MIME or understand the format. A minimal implementation simply strips out all formatting commands and parameter sections, leaving only readable plain text. This "degradation" is far preferable to binary formats that become useless gibberish on non-conformant systems.

The format is designed to be extensible: software can define new formatting commands and private extensions using the X- prefix (following the convention of Internet mail headers). The <param> mechanism allows extensions to include command-specific parameters without breaking compatibility. Mail systems can include text/enriched in a multipart/alternative body with other formats, allowing sophisticated readers to choose the best version while others fall back to plain text.
sections.eli5: If a mail system does not understand enriched text, it can just ignore the tags and show plain text. New features can be added without breaking old systems.

sections.title: Character Sets and Non-ASCII Text
sections.content:
Text/enriched defaults to US-ASCII but can specify other character sets via a charset parameter. For single-byte character sets like ISO-8859 (Latin-1), this works straightforwardly: the less-than octet can be quoted as before. For multibyte character sets like ISO-2022, the RFC specifies that text should be switched back into ASCII before processing formatting commands, so the octet value 60 is reliably recognized as a command delimiter.

The RFC acknowledges that hypothetical future character sets that do not subsume ASCII would pose problems but defers addressing them, as no such widely-used sets existed at the time of writing. The approach taken is pragmatic: ensure text/enriched works with the character sets actually in use without over-engineering for theoretical future needs.
sections.eli5: The format works with different languages and character sets. Commands are always in regular ASCII so they work everywhere.

data.title: Sample text/enriched
data.code:
<bold>Now</bold> is the time for <italic>all</italic>
good men and <smaller>(and women)</smaller> to
come to the aid of their country.
